   - `risk_of_bias_tool`: Pick the single design-matched tool per `RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1:

     * `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"` (quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without quasi-experimental intervention comparator)

     * `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"` (legal-empirical, doctrinal-empirical, jurimetric, or institutional-historical study that fits none of the six conventional designs above)

evidence_quotes.quote: We put together a unique panel data of 208 urban water utilities
controlling for utility and year ﬁxed effects and lags of utility and city variables
employment by about 9% and lowered the managerial expense as a share of
domestic water users increases with PSP or PSP majority.

evidence_quotes.criterion: mechanism_certainty and water service evidence limitation
evidence_quotes.quote: Reliable evidence on how water utility privatization affects water supply services in

country.comment: Urban water utilities and prefecture-level/direct-governance cities across China.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Section I; PDF p. 6–7, Section III

effect_estimate.comment: Reports exact panel fixed-effects estimates for city-level water supply and user coverage (Table 8) as well as utility-level operational, financial, and subsidy indicators (Tables 5–7).
effect_estimate.value: In two-way fixed-effects panel models with lagged utility and city controls (Table 8), general private sector participation (PSP; any nonstate capital share) had no statistically significant effect on log total urban water supply (-0.020, SE 0.026 in original coding; -0.038, SE 0.030 in corrective recoding; N = 1,752), log urban domestic water supply (-0.054, SE 0.044; -0.044, SE 0.052; N = 814), or log domestic water supply population (+0.026, SE 0.025; +0.037, SE 0.026; N = 814). Disaggregating by ownership share, majority PSP (>50% nonstate capital) was marginally associated with lower log urban domestic water supply in original coding (-0.071, SE 0.038, p < 0.10; -0.062, SE 0.047 in corrective recoding; N = 814) and higher log domestic water supply population in corrective recoding (+0.046, SE 0.026, p < 0.10, ~4.6% more domestic users; +0.032, SE 0.026 in original coding; N = 814), whereas minority PSP showed no significant effects. At the utility level (Tables 5–7, full controls), PSP significantly reduced log employment (-0.0918, SE 0.0404, p < 0.05, N = 1,547) and managerial expense-to-sales ratio (-0.0274, SE 0.0145, p < 0.10, N = 1,752), driven by majority PSP (employment: -0.113, SE 0.0348, p < 0.01 in original coding; -0.119, SE 0.0399, p < 0.01 in corrective recoding; managerial expense ratio: -0.0213, SE 0.0107, p < 0.05; profit-sales ratio: +0.0411, SE 0.0213, p < 0.10 in original coding and +0.0714, SE 0.0336, p < 0.05 in corrective recoding, N = 1,515), with no statistically significant change in subsidy-sales ratio (-0.00917, SE 0.00868, N = 1,752).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 21–22, Section V.B & Table 5; PDF p. 24–25, Table 6; PDF p. 26–30, Sections V.C–V.D & Tables 7–8

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (documented statistical association). Although appraised under ROBINS-I as a longitudinal policy/ownership fixed-effects study, overall risk of bias is Serious due to endogenous bidirectional PSP entry and exit driven by unobserved local government commitments, misclassification of BOT/TOT/divestiture utilities as state-owned controls (PDF p. 11), indirect recovery of domestic user counts from city yearbooks, and substantial missing data on domestic water outcomes (N = 814 of 2,072 observations), precluding a rating of 3. Furthermore, regulatory and administrative mechanisms (tariff hearings, provincial tariff approvals, concession enforcement, leakage reduction) are not directly observed in the dataset, and city-level water supply/user associations are mostly null or marginally significant at the 10% level.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 11, Section IV.A; PDF p. 13–14, Section IV.A; PDF p. 27 & 30–31, Section V.D, Table 8 & Section VI

mechanism_flags.comment: The primary empirical variable is corporate private sector equity participation (PSP, majority vs. minority nonstate capital ownership) in urban water utilities rather than household-level ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, or ENFORCEMENT barriers. Substantively, Sections IV.A and VI examine regulatory fragmentation (absence of an integrated national legal/regulatory framework resulting in localized case-by-case concession/equity deals) and intergovernmental political/regulatory coordination (tensions between municipal government return/sales commitments, central bans on guaranteed returns, and provincial approval authority over water tariffs). Regulated tariffs (fees) and public tariff hearings (participation) are discussed qualitatively as institutional context (PDF p. 13–14, 31) but are not measured in the empirical analysis.
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 9–11 & 13–14, Section IV.A; PDF p. 17, Section IV.B; PDF p. 31, Section VI

outcome_flags.comment: Section V.D and Table 8 empirically analyze city-level total urban water supply and total urban domestic water supply (service_quantity) and the number of urban domestic water users / domestic water supply population as a measure of utility service coverage (service_coverage). Leakage, water quality, pressure, and retail water tariffs/affordability are explicitly noted as not available in the dataset (PDF p. 27, 31).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 9, Section III; PDF p. 27, Section V.D; PDF p. 30, Table 8; PDF p. 32, Appendix Table A1

publication_year.comment: Explicitly printed in the copyright and electronic publication footer on the first page.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Non-randomized longitudinal quasi-experimental evaluation of utility privatization / private sector participation (PSP) versus state-owned water utilities using two-way (utility and year) fixed-effects panel regressions and dynamic Arellano-Bond panel estimators with lagged selection controls and a falsification test. Matches ROBINS-I per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 16–20, Section IV.B & Section V.A; PDF p. 25, Section V.B; PDF p. 27, Section V.D

sample_size.comment: Panel of 208 large and medium urban water utilities across 192 prefecture-level and direct-governance cities from 1998 to 2007 (summarized as 'about 200 Chinese cities' in the Introduction, with exact final matched sample reported as 208 utilities in 192 cities in Section III). Regression sample sizes vary by variable availability from N = 772 to N = 2,072 utility-year observations (N = 1,752 for total urban water supply; N = 814 for urban domestic water supply and domestic water supply population).
sample_size.value: 208 urban water utilities in 192 cities (1998–2007 panel; up to 2,072 utility-year observations; N = 1,752 observations for urban water supply and N = 814 observations for urban domestic water supply and domestic water supply population)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 7, Section III; PDF p. 12, Table 1; PDF p. 19, Table 4; PDF p. 22, Table 5; PDF p. 30, Table 8

study_design.comment: Observational longitudinal panel econometric evaluation comparing utilities with private/nonstate capital participation (overall, majority, and minority PSP) against wholly state-owned water utilities over 10 years, modeling selection into PSP and controlling for utility and year fixed effects and lagged covariates.
study_design.value: Longitudinal quasi-experimental panel study (1998–2007) using two-way utility and year fixed-effects models, Arellano-Bond dynamic panel estimators, and random-effects probit / linear fixed-effects selection models
